title: What is the difference between a Flink checkpoint and a savepoint (automatic fault-tolerance snapshot vs user-triggered, externally-stored, version-portable snapshot for upgrades/rescaling/topology changes)?

s1_definition.profdef: Checkpoints and savepoints are both consistent snapshots of a Flink job's state, but they serve different purposes and have different lifecycles. A checkpoint is an automatic, periodic snapshot taken and owned by Flink purely for fault tolerance; it is optimized for low overhead, may use an incremental format tied to the state backend, and is typically deleted automatically when superseded or when the job finishes. A savepoint is a user-triggered snapshot stored in a stable, self-contained, version-portable format designed for operational actions such as upgrading the job's code, changing its parallelism, migrating state, or performing planned restarts; it is owned by the user and persists until explicitly deleted. In short, checkpoints are for automatic recovery, savepoints are for intentional lifecycle operations.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India's processing system takes two kinds of backups. A checkpoint is like the automatic, frequent autosave the system makes every few seconds purely so that if the power trips it can recover to a moment ago; nobody asks for it, it is optimized to be cheap, and old autosaves are discarded as new ones appear. A savepoint is like a deliberate, labeled full export the operations team requests before they upgrade the software, add more servers, or reorganize the processing stages; it is a clean, portable archive the team names and keeps, and they can restore from it into the new version of the system. Checkpoints keep the lights on automatically, while savepoints are the planned, human-driven milestones.
s1_definition.oneliner: Checkpoints are Flink's automatic, cheap, self-owned snapshots for crash recovery, while savepoints are user-triggered, portable, durable snapshots for upgrades, rescaling, and planned changes.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Checkpoints and savepoints are both consistent snapshots of a Flink job's state, but they serve different purposes and have different lifecycles. A checkpoint is an automatic, periodic snapshot taken and owned by Flink purely for fault tolerance; it is optimized for low overhead, may use an incremental format tied to the state backend, and is typically deleted automatically when superseded or when the job finishes. A savepoint is a user-triggered snapshot stored in a stable, self-contained, version-portable format designed for operational actions such as upgrading the job's code, changing its parallelism, migrating state, or performing planned restarts; it is owned by the user and persists until explicitly deleted. In short, checkpoints are for automatic recovery, savepoints are for intentional lifecycle operations.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India's processing system takes two kinds of backups. A checkpoint is like the automatic, frequent autosave the system makes every few seconds purely so that if the power trips it can recover to a moment ago; nobody asks for it, it is optimized to be cheap, and old autosaves are discarded as new ones appear. A savepoint is like a deliberate, labeled full export the operations team requests before they upgrade the software, add more servers, or reorganize the processing stages; it is a clean, portable archive the team names and keeps, and they can restore from it into the new version of the system. Checkpoints keep the lights on automatically, while savepoints are the planned, human-driven milestones.

**One line to remember:** Checkpoints are Flink's automatic, cheap, self-owned snapshots for crash recovery, while savepoints are user-triggered, portable, durable snapshots for upgrades, rescaling, and planned changes.

sections.s2_technical:
Checkpoints are triggered automatically by the checkpoint coordinator on the interval you configure with `env.enableCheckpointing(10_000)`. They are owned and managed by Flink, which decides when to create and delete them. By default a checkpoint is cleaned up when a newer one completes or when the job stops, though you can configure retention with `ExternalizedCheckpointCleanup` so a checkpoint survives job cancellation for emergency recovery. Checkpoints prioritize low overhead: with the RocksDB backend they can be incremental, uploading only changed state files, which makes them cheap enough to run frequently. Their format can be tied to the state backend and the exact job, so they are not guaranteed to be portable across Flink versions or across changes to the job's operators.

Savepoints are triggered manually by an operator, for example `flink savepoint <jobId> <path>` or `flink stop --savepoint <path> <jobId>` to stop with a final savepoint. They are written in a canonical, self-contained, stable format specifically designed to be portable: you can restore a savepoint into a job whose code has changed, whose parallelism is different, or that is running a newer Flink version, as long as operators are matched by their assigned unique IDs. Savepoints are owned by the user and are never automatically deleted; you keep them as long as you need and remove them explicitly. Because they prioritize portability and completeness over speed, taking a savepoint can be heavier than an incremental checkpoint.

The crucial operational distinction is intent. You rely on checkpoints transparently for automatic fault tolerance; if a task manager dies, Flink restores from the latest completed checkpoint without you doing anything. You use savepoints for deliberate lifecycle operations: deploying a new version of the application, rescaling the job to more or fewer slots, changing the topology such as adding or modifying operators, or migrating state across clusters. The senior nuances are several. Assign stable unique IDs to your operators with `uid(...)`, because savepoint restore matches state to operators by those IDs, and without them a code change can orphan state and fail the restore. In newer Flink versions the distinction has blurred somewhat because retained checkpoints can also be used to resume and native-format savepoints exist for speed, but the conceptual split remains: checkpoints for automatic recovery, savepoints for intentional operations. You should also test savepoint-restore as part of your deployment pipeline, because a broken state migration discovered in production during an upgrade is extremely costly for a bank.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a long-lived fraud-scoring job that accumulates per-account state. If a task manager crashes at 3 a.m., the job must recover on its own to the most recent consistent moment without any human intervention, losing at most a few seconds of progress. This is exactly the role of automatic checkpoints: cheap, frequent, Flink-owned snapshots used transparently for crash recovery.

Problem 2 — The same bank needs to deploy an improved fraud model that adds a new operator and increase the job's parallelism to handle growth, all without losing the accumulated per-account state. The team must take a clean, portable snapshot, stop the old job, and start the new version from that snapshot even though the code and parallelism changed. This is exactly the role of a savepoint: a user-triggered, portable snapshot for an upgrade and rescale, with operators matched by their stable unique IDs.

In the mini-project we build a runnable demo that models both lifecycles. We define a `JobState` holding per-account fraud scores and the operator unique IDs that own them. A `CheckpointManager` automatically snapshots on an interval, keeps only the latest, and can restore after a simulated crash. A `SavepointManager` takes a user-triggered snapshot into a named, retained location, keeps all of them, and can restore into a job whose version and parallelism differ, matching state by operator uid. A `CheckpointVsSavepointDemo` main class runs the job, shows automatic checkpoints superseding each other and recovering from a crash, then takes a savepoint, upgrades the job to a new version with higher parallelism, and restores from the savepoint to show the state carried across the change.

Configuration file:

```yaml
# application.yml
flink:
  checkpoint:
    interval-ms: 5000
    externalized-retention: RETAIN_ON_CANCELLATION
    storage: s3://nbi-flink/checkpoints
  savepoint:
    dir: s3://nbi-flink/savepoints
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a fraud-scoring job with a single operator whose unique id is fraud-scoring-op, processing a few transactions, taking automatic checkpoints, recovering from a crash, then being upgraded via a savepoint with a parallelism change from two to six.

Step 1: The job scores Rajesh by 10 and takes an automatic checkpoint. The checkpoint manager records checkpoint one with the current scores. This is Flink's own periodic snapshot, taken without anyone asking.

Step 2: The job scores Priya by 5 and takes another automatic checkpoint. The checkpoint manager records checkpoint two and supersedes checkpoint one, keeping only the latest, which is how checkpoints stay cheap and self-managing.

Step 3: A crash is simulated. Flink automatically restores from the latest checkpoint, bringing back Rajesh at 10 and Priya at 5 without any human action. The job resumes processing from that consistent moment, demonstrating the fault-tolerance role of checkpoints.

Step 4: After recovery the job scores Rajesh by another 20, so Rajesh is now 30 and Priya is 5 in the live state. The team now wants to deploy an improved model and add capacity.

Step 5: The operator takes a user-triggered savepoint into a named, retained path. The savepoint manager stores a portable snapshot tagged with the operator unique id fraud-scoring-op, capturing Rajesh 30 and Priya 5. Unlike checkpoints, this savepoint is kept until explicitly deleted.

Step 6: A new job version is started with the same operator unique id but parallelism raised to six, restoring from the savepoint. Because the operator ids match, the state is correctly re-homed into the new job, so Rajesh comes back as 30 and the upgraded model continues, scoring Rajesh by one more to 31. The demo proves checkpoints handle automatic recovery while a savepoint carried the state across a deliberate upgrade and rescale.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Checkpoints and savepoints are both consistent snapshots of a Flink job's state, but they exist for different reasons and have different lifecycles, and confusing them is a common mistake. A checkpoint is an automatic, periodic snapshot taken and owned by Flink purely for fault tolerance. The checkpoint coordinator triggers it on your configured interval, it is optimized to be cheap, often incremental with the RocksDB backend so it uploads only changed state, and by default it is cleaned up automatically when a newer one completes or when the job stops, though you can retain it on cancellation for emergencies. Its format can be tied to the state backend and the exact job, so it is not guaranteed to be portable across Flink versions or across changes to the operators. You never think about checkpoints during normal operation; if a task manager dies, Flink silently restores from the latest completed checkpoint and resumes.

A savepoint, by contrast, is a user-triggered snapshot written in a stable, self-contained, portable format designed specifically for deliberate lifecycle operations. You take it explicitly, for example with a stop-with-savepoint command, and it is owned by you and retained until you delete it. Its whole purpose is portability: you can restore a savepoint into a job whose code has changed, whose parallelism is different, or that runs a newer Flink version, as long as your operators carry stable unique IDs, because savepoint restore matches state to operators by those IDs. That is why assigning a uid to every stateful operator is essential, since without it a code change can orphan state and break the restore. Savepoints prioritize completeness and portability over speed, so they can be heavier than an incremental checkpoint. The short version is: checkpoints for automatic recovery, savepoints for intentional operations like upgrades, rescaling, and topology changes.

At the National Bank of India this distinction was part of our daily operations. Our long-lived fraud-scoring job ran with checkpoints every few seconds so that an overnight task-manager crash recovered on its own to a moment earlier with no human involvement, which is exactly what you want for reliability. When we needed to deploy an improved fraud model that added an operator and to scale the job up for growth, we did not rely on checkpoints; we took a savepoint, stopped the old job, and started the new version from that savepoint with higher parallelism, and because every stateful operator had a stable uid, the accumulated per-account scores carried cleanly into the new topology. We also made savepoint-restore part of our deployment testing, because discovering a broken state migration in production during an upgrade would be unacceptable for a bank. Being able to explain that checkpoints are cheap, automatic, and Flink-owned for crash recovery, while savepoints are portable, retained, and user-owned for planned changes, and to stress the role of operator uids, is exactly the operational maturity an interviewer is probing for.
